card-tricks.seoDescription: General card tricks explained step by step in plain English, with a pointer to every other kind of trick on the site: easy, impromptu, mental and more.
card-tricks.intro:
This is the catch-all shelf. When a trick doesn't fit neatly anywhere else, or fits everywhere at once, it lands here. Right now the star of the shelf is [The Mirrored Mind Reader](/mirrored-mind-reader-card-trick/), a lovely piece where you seem to read a spectator's thoughts using nothing but a shuffled deck and a quietly remembered key card.

Who is it for? Honestly, anyone with a deck in their hand and ten minutes to spare. You don't need special cards or fancy moves. What you do need is a little patience: read the whole trick once, then walk through it slowly with the cards in front of you, then do it again without looking at the page.

Most of the tricks on this site lean on a handful of old ideas. A card you secretly know, a pile that gets dealt in a clever order, a choice that isn't really a choice. Once you spot those ideas you'll start seeing them everywhere, and you'll be able to invent your own variations.

If you're just getting started, I'd head over to [Easy Tricks](/category/easy-tricks/) or [Self-Working Tricks](/category/self-working-tricks/) first. If you like the mind-reading feel of the Mirrored Mind Reader, the [Mental Tricks](/category/mental-tricks/) page is full of them. And if a word in any write-up puzzles you, the [glossary](/glossary/) should help.

easy-tricks.seoDescription: Easy card tricks for beginners, explained step by step. No sleight of hand, just an ordinary deck, a little practice and a good story to tell.
easy-tricks.intro:
These are the tricks I'd hand to a friend who has never done a card trick in their life. None of them need sleight of hand. Most work with any borrowed deck, and the hardest part is usually remembering a card or keeping a straight face.

What makes them tick is almost always one of a few simple ideas: a card you peeked at on the bottom of the deck, a few cards secretly placed before you start, or a count that always ends in the same spot. The magic comes from the way you present it. A trick like [The 3 Thieves](/the-3-thieves/) or [Kings Robbery](/kings-robbery-2/) is really a little story with cards as the actors, and the story does most of the fooling.

To practice, read a trick through once, then do it slowly at the table with the page open. Do it three or four times on your own before you show anyone. Say your lines out loud, too. It feels silly, but it's how you find the bits where you stumble.

Good ones to start with are [The Bottom Card](/the-bottom-card/), which teaches you the most useful secret in card magic, and [Magic 21](/magic-21/), a classic that works itself. Once these feel easy, the [Self-Working Tricks](/category/self-working-tricks/) and [Impromptu Tricks](/category/impromptu-tricks/) are the natural next step.

expert-tricks.seoDescription: Expert card tricks for practiced hands: double lifts, palms, controls and faro shuffles, explained step by step for when the easy tricks feel too easy.
expert-tricks.intro:
This is where the real hand work lives. If you've been through the easy and intermediate tricks and want something that will fool people who think they know how card tricks work, start here. Fair warning: these take weeks, not minutes.

The tricks on this page lean on proper sleights. You'll meet the double lift, palming a card, holding a pinky break, controlling a chosen card to the top, and even the faro shuffle. None of them are magic on their own. What makes them deceptive is doing them smoothly, at the same pace as your ordinary handling, so nothing looks different when the secret move happens.

Practice in front of a mirror, and practice the sleight on its own before you try the full routine. I like to do a move a hundred times while watching TV, until my hands do it without me thinking. Then go back to the trick.

[The Ambitious Card](/the-ambitious-card/) is the one every card magician should learn, and it's a great home for your double lift. [The Color Transfer](/the-color-transfer/) is a short, sharp visual. [Always On Top](/always-on-top/) is a proper workout for your palm, and [Aces for Cardmen Only](/aces-for-cardmen-only/) is the faro routine to aim for. If any of this feels like too much, step back to the [Intermediate Tricks](/category/intermediate-tricks/) for a while. There's no shame in it.

impromptu-tricks.seoDescription: Impromptu card tricks you can do anytime with a borrowed deck. No setup and no gimmicks, so you are ready the moment someone says show me a trick.
impromptu-tricks.intro:
These are my favorite kind of tricks: the ones you can do right now. Somebody slides a deck across the table and says "show me something," and you can. No setup, no special cards, no running off to the other room to arrange anything first.

Because you can't prepare the deck, impromptu tricks have to create their secrets in front of everyone. You glimpse the bottom card while you shuffle, you secretly flip a card while the spectator looks at theirs, or you let the spectator's own counting do the work. The trick is to make those moments look like nothing at all.

The best way to practice is to carry a deck around for a week and do your chosen trick for anyone who'll watch. Family is fine. You'll learn more from five real performances than from fifty in front of the mirror.

A few to try: [Back Flip](/back-flip/) makes a card jump out of the deck face up, and it's great with kids. [After Drinks](/after-drinks/) has you toss the deck onto a chair and still come up with their two cards. [Slap Happy](/slap-happy/) ends with a satisfying slap that leaves only the chosen card in your hand, and [Cutting the Aces](/cutting-the-aces/) is a lovely showpiece once you've got the hang of a finger break. Many of the [Easy Tricks](/category/easy-tricks/) are impromptu too, and when you're ready for more, try the [Intermediate Tricks](/category/intermediate-tricks/).

intermediate-tricks.seoDescription: Intermediate card tricks that ask a little more of you: simple sleights, longer routines and stronger effects, all explained step by step in plain English.
intermediate-tricks.intro:
These are for when the easy tricks start to feel easy. You've got a few tricks you can do in your sleep, people have stopped asking "do it again," and you want something with a bit more punch.

The step up here is mostly about two things. First, a few simple moves: a palm, a finger break, a false shuffle that keeps a card where you want it. Second, longer routines with more than one phase, where the spectator thinks the trick is over and then it isn't. You'll also find clever counting and mathematical principles dressed up as mind reading.

Learn the trick in pieces. Get the method right with the cards face up, so you can see what's happening. Then turn them face down and add your patter. Only then speed up. A slow, confident trick beats a fast, nervous one every time.

Some I'm especially fond of: [The Changing Card](/the-changing-card/) is a perfect first palming trick. [Teleporting Aces](/teleporting-aces/) and [Trapped Trick](/trapped-trick/) are strong visual pieces, and [The Year Game](/the-year-game/) is a math trick that feels like real magic. If you want gentler material, the [Easy Tricks](/category/easy-tricks/) are always there. If you're hungry for more, the [Expert Tricks](/category/expert-tricks/) are waiting.

math-tricks.seoDescription: Mathematical card tricks that work by counting, dealing and simple arithmetic. Learn why they work, then present them so they feel like real magic.
math-tricks.intro:
If you liked puzzles at school, you'll love this page. Every trick here works because of a bit of arithmetic hiding in plain sight: a count that always comes out the same, piles that add up to a number you already know, or a deal that quietly moves a card to a fixed position.

The nice thing about math tricks is that they can't go wrong if you follow the steps. The hard part is making them not feel like a math lesson. Nobody is amazed by subtraction. So keep the counting brisk, give the spectator something to do, and put your energy into the reveal.

Practice these face up first. Watch where the important card goes during each deal and count along. Once you understand why it works, you'll stop worrying about it, and that makes you a much more relaxed performer.

[The Year Game](/the-year-game/) is a great one to start with. [Kathy's Prediction](/kathys-prediction/) turns a simple count into a prediction, and [The Lazy Magician](/the-lazy-magician/) lets the spectator do all the work while you take the credit. [Mental Agility](/mental-agility/) works with any pack. Many math tricks are also [Self-Working Tricks](/category/self-working-tricks/), and the [Memory Tricks](/category/memory-tricks/) page has a few more number-crunchers.

memory-tricks.seoDescription: Card tricks built on memory: stacked decks, mnemonics and remembered cards. Learn simple systems that let you name any card the spectator picks.
memory-tricks.intro:
These tricks ask you to remember something: a card, a short list, or, in the bigger ones, the order of a whole deck. It sounds like a lot, but the systems here are made for ordinary memories like mine. A silly sentence and a made-up word are often all you need.

The most famous example is the old "eight kings" stack in [Chased](/chased/). You learn one rhyme for the values and the word CHaSeD for the suits, arrange the deck to match, and from then on a single peek at one card tells you the next. Once it's in your head, it stays there, and it powers dozens of tricks.

Practice the memory part away from the cards. Say the rhyme on your walk, in the shower, while waiting for the kettle. When you can rattle it off without thinking, then pick up the deck. Trying to remember and perform at the same time is where things fall apart.

Also worth a look: [What's on Your Mind?](/whats-on-your-mind/), where you remember four cards and pull the thought-of one from your pocket, [Triple Threat](/triple-threat/), and [The Impossible Location](/impossible-location-card-trick/), which mixes memory with a touch of mentalism. If you enjoy these, the [Mental Tricks](/category/mental-tricks/) and [Math Tricks](/category/math-tricks/) pages are close cousins.

mental-tricks.seoDescription: Mind-reading card tricks and mentalism effects: predictions, secret codes with a partner and cards named without looking, all explained step by step.
mental-tricks.intro:
These are the tricks where you don't just find the card, you seem to read it straight out of someone's head. Mind reading, predictions and a little bit of theater. They're some of the strongest things you can do with a deck, because the spectator never sees you do anything.

Behind the curtain, the methods are often simple. A glimpsed card, a choice that only looks free, a prediction you write after you already know the answer, or a friend who knows a secret code. In tricks like [ESP](/esp/) and [On Tap](/on-tap/) your partner leaves the room and still picks out the right card, thanks to a signal nobody notices.

What really sells mental tricks is your manner. Slow down. Look at the spectator, not the cards. Act like it's hard work, and occasionally get a detail "almost" right before you nail it. Practice the talking as much as the method, and if you're working with a partner, rehearse your signals until they're invisible.

Start with [Mind Reader](/mind-reader/), which uses a sneaky choice that always lands where you want, then try [Psychic Prediction](/psychic-prediction/) and [The Predictive Ace](/predictive-ace-card-trick/). For tricks that lean more on remembering than reading, have a look at [Memory Tricks](/category/memory-tricks/).

self-working-tricks.seoDescription: Self-working card tricks that do the hard part for you. No sleight of hand, just follow the steps, practice your patter and let the method do its job.
self-working-tricks.intro:
Self-working tricks are the closest thing in magic to a free lunch. You follow the steps, the deck does the work, and the trick happens. No sleight of hand, no secret moves, and very little that can go wrong.

That doesn't mean they're dull. Some of the cleverest ideas in card magic are self-working. They rely on counting, dealing into piles, the way cards move during a cut, or a bit of setup done before anyone is watching. Because the method is automatic, all your attention can go into the presentation, and that's where these tricks really shine.

I'd practice a self-working trick in two passes. First, run it face up a few times to see why it works. It's satisfying, and it means you won't panic if something feels off. Second, practice the story. Give the spectator a reason to deal, cut or spell, and the trick feels like theirs.

[Magic 21](/magic-21/) is the classic everyone should know. [All the Aces](/all-the-aces/) has the spectator find all four aces themselves. [The Hotel](/the-hotel/) is a story trick that kids love, and [Lucky 13](/lucky-13/) is a good one for a fresh deck. If you like knowing why things work, you'll enjoy the [Math Tricks](/category/math-tricks/), and the [Easy Tricks](/category/easy-tricks/) page has plenty more for beginners.
